routes.description: Establish that determinism and indeterminism both fail to provide the conscious authorship and same-circumstances alternatives integral to free will, and that practical capacities or accountability conventions do not supply what is missing.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if unauthored causes, constitutive luck, and unconscious processes defeat ultimate authorship while randomness supplies no control, leaving compatibilist competence and social regulation unable to establish free will in the disputed sense.

motionBridge.description: Show that neither causal determination nor indeterminacy permits the authorship and alternative possibilities required for free will and ultimate moral responsibility.

centralBridges.description: Establish that preserving useful capacities under the name free will omits the first-person authorship and actual ability to have done otherwise that motivate the dispute.
Show that genes, environment, prior brain states, and unconscious processes produce character and choice without being authored by the agent.
Distinguish useful accountability and behavioral regulation from genuine authorship or ultimate moral responsibility for causally produced conduct.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that tracing conduct to earlier choices only moves the authorship problem backward, while microscopic contingencies expose pervasive causal luck.
Show that randomness adds no ownership and that sufficiently informative advance prediction would expose rather than create conscious authorship.

routes.description: Establish that freedom worth preserving is the graded, naturalistic competence to deliberate, respond to reasons, exercise self-control, and undertake obligations, none of which requires exemption from deterministic causation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if reasons-responsive control supports meaningful agency and calibrated responsibility, while demands for absolute self-creation, exact-replay alternatives, or indeterministic choice are shown unnecessary to the distinctions and practices free will must preserve.

motionBridge.description: Show that reasons-responsive agency supplies a determinism-compatible form of freedom sufficient for meaningful control and moral responsibility.

centralBridges.description: Define free agency through functioning capacities for reflection, ordered desire, attention, self-control, learning, and responsiveness to reasons.
Show that genuine control and temporally extended authorship do not require control of every background condition or awareness of every implementing microprocess.
Ground responsibility in graded competence, obligations, justified reliance, and stable consequentialist practices rather than absolute metaphysical desert.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain ability to do otherwise through robust competencies and relevantly similar circumstances rather than atom-for-atom replay of the universe.
Show that quantum indeterminacy adds no morally relevant freedom unavailable from deterministic deliberation, control, and practical randomness.

sections.title: The Concept and Stakes of Free Will
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether naturalistic conceptual revision preserves the phenomenon at stake or changes the subject by omitting authorship and same-circumstances alternatives.

sections.title: Reasons-Responsive Competence and Bounded Control
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether deliberation, self-control, obligations, and responsiveness to reasons constitute genuine agency despite dependence on uncontrolled causal conditions.

sections.title: Authorship, Constitutive Luck, and Neural Causation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether genes, environment, prior brain states, anomalous lapses, and unconscious implementation defeat authorship or remain compatible with temporally extended self-governance.

sections.title: Alternative Possibilities, Replay, and Randomness
sections.rationale: This issue compares exact-replay ability with competence across relevantly similar circumstances and tests whether deterministic chaos or indeterminacy contributes anything morally significant.

sections.title: Moral Responsibility, Accountability, and Social Practice
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether causal explanation universally exculpates or whether graded competence, reliance, deterrence, rehabilitation, and stable institutions sustain responsibility without absolute authorship.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: The freedom relevant to moral responsibility is compatible with determinism, whereas libertarian or indeterminist freedom is an unnecessary philosophical fantasy.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn follows the explicit handoff to Dennett and consistently presents his compatibilist position in the first person.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly frames the compatibilist route by identifying responsibility-supporting freedom, rather than indeterminist freedom, as the phenomenon requiring preservation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states the governing distinction clearly and directly organizes the ensuing compatibilist case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The central compatibility claim is recoverable and stable, though the sufficiency standard for moral responsibility remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The confident dismissal of libertarian freedom exceeds the compressed support, while the compatibility thesis is presented as a defended position.

charity.alternative: Libertarian freedom might target ultimate authorship rather than merely useful responsibility-supporting capacities.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move prioritizes responsibility but does not yet show that this preserves the disputed authorship phenomenon.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between two freedom claims is coherent, with one bounded implicit bridge from responsibility relevance to conceptual priority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The passage supplies a clear philosophical distinction but little support for treating one conception as dispensable.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion-level claim that responsibility-relevant freedom can coexist with determinism.

representationalCharity.rationale: It identifies the rival conception accurately but dismisses its importance before fully engaging its authorship motivation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly separates incompatibility from moral-responsibility relevance and calls the latter the variety worth wanting.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Compatibilism can preserve a naturalistic concept of free will by discarding inherited magical commitments without discarding the real phenomenon those commitments misdescribe.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage begins with Dennett explicitly stating his view of compatibilism and remains his sustained answer until Harris begins responding in the final row.

response.rationale: This constructive move presents compatibilism as a naturalistic recovery project that removes magical commitments while retaining the real functional phenomenon.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies a useful conceptual orientation, although the preserved phenomenon is only partly specified here.

precisionFindings.rationale: The revisionary thesis is clear, but terms such as theology, magic, and the real phenomenon remain partly programmatic.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The characterization is plausible but more confident than the excerpt's limited explanation of what is retained warrants.

charity.alternative: The incompatibilist may accept naturalism while arguing that compatibilism changes the subject rather than removing magical residue.
charity.decisiveQualification: A naturalistic revision must identify which motivating features survive and which are legitimately abandoned.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A coherent revisionary program is offered, but the bridge from anti-magical naturalism to preservation of the same phenomenon is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies mainly on characterization and does not yet document the functional features supposedly preserved.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports motion-level compatibilist preservation by describing how the concept can be naturalized.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the rival as anti-theological but too quickly treats that stance as misunderstanding compatibilism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls compatibilism the opposite of theology and begins an account of examining what the phenomenon actually is.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Responsible agency consists in graded capacities including ordered desires, flexible attention, responsiveness to reasons, and self-control, which distinguish free from impaired agents regardless of determinism.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett continues his uninterrupted explanation, poses a question about ideal responsibility, and supplies a detailed answer in his own theoretical vocabulary.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the central positive account of responsible agency through graded cognitive, motivational, and self-control capacities.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it gives the most explicit and practically discriminating statement of the reasons-responsive competence package.

precisionFindings.rationale: The capacities are enumerated, their graded character is explicit, and the proposition's scope is readily recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately qualifies agency as graded and does not claim that every adult possesses the capacities equally.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The listed capacities form a consistent and explicit functional account with no material internal gap in the local inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific capacities and impairment-sensitive gradation support the account, though comparative defense against authorship objections is deferred.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It very directly supplies the indispensable central bridge defining competent reasons-responsive control.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage develops a positive competence model without materially interpreting or characterizing an opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names true beliefs, ordered desires, flexible attention, responsiveness to reasons, and self-control, expressly noting degrees.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Compatibilism omits the first-person authorship and same-circumstances ability to do otherwise that motivate the free-will problem, preserving useful capacities under the name of a different phenomenon.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris begins by qualifying his agreement with Dennett and then speaks continuously through his phenomenological account and extended Atlantis analogy.

components.text: Whether responsibility-relevant capacities preserve the first-person authorship and same-circumstances freedom motivating the dispute.
Whether naturalistic revision preserves the original phenomenon or replaces it with a different functional construct.
Whether a package of graded capacities alone answers the first-person authorship demand.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges conceptual preservation by distinguishing first- and third-person descriptions and alleging equivocation between them, but it does not deny the reality of the listed competence package.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a strong partial answer contacting the decisive conceptual-preservation issue while leaving the detailed competence account largely intact.

precisionFindings.rationale: The first-person versus third-person distinction is clear, though the scope of what ordinary people uniformly feel is somewhat broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents the phenomenological claim as a general tendency and explicitly explains the risk of moving between perspectives.

charity.alternative: Compatibilism may deliberately revise folk phenomenology while preserving the capacities that justify responsibility.
charity.decisiveQualification: That revision still must explain why omitting same-circumstances authorship does not change the subject.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The change-of-subject challenge follows coherently from the two-perspective distinction, with a bounded assumption about conceptual motivation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The phenomenological distinction and analogy support the claim, but broad claims about what people feel lack representative evidence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central conceptual-target bridge by specifying what compatibilist revision may omit.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly concedes useful capacities and targets the narrower question whether they preserve the phenomenon under dispute.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly distinguishes first-person and third-person descriptions and warns that unnoticed movement between them loses important details.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: When a minute synaptic condition can redirect a consequential choice and an entire life, the agent's dependence on unauthored physical causes undermines the ordinary picture of autonomous authorship.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris explicitly agrees before marking what Dennett has not acknowledged, then develops the first-person challenge through examples involving marriage and life-changing decisions.

components.text: Whether reasons-responsive capacities amount to authorship when their neural implementation depends on minute unauthored physical conditions.
Whether determinism-compatible responsibility survives the return of causal marionette strings at decisive choice points.

response.rationale: The move contacts the authorship implication of the competence account by arguing that microscopic neural dependence can redirect major choices, although it does not dispute that capacities distinguish agents.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive implication but only partially answers the functional compatibilist claim because dependence alone is not shown to eliminate control.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal-dependence claim is clear, but the leap from possible synaptic difference to pervasive nonauthorship needs a scope qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The counterfactual examples are framed conditionally, appropriately acknowledging that the microscopic causal story is illustrative.

charity.alternative: A compatibilist can accept complete neural implementation while locating control in the organized agent-level process.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must show why microphysical dependence defeats rather than implements high-level control.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The example establishes possible causal sensitivity, but the bridge from sensitivity to loss of autonomous authorship remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The synaptic example is vivid yet speculative and lacks support showing that such tiny variations commonly decide consequential actions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central causal-nonauthorship bridge by linking choice to unauthored neural conditions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move exposes causal dependence but does not fully engage the strongest realization-based account of agent-level control.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says that a different synaptic charge could alter marriage or participation and describes this as restoring marionette strings.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Microscopic neural variation can determine life-changing actions even when a decision is not already balanced on a knife-edge, so causal chance cannot be confined to inconsequential toss-ups.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly marks Harris's disagreement with Dennett and continues uninterrupted until Dennett answers with the voting example.

components.text: Whether consequential action is reliably governed by stable competence rather than microscopic variation outside the agent's control.

response.rationale: The move challenges confinement of microscopic variation to evenly balanced decisions, but it offers a probabilistic counterexample rather than a full account of why competence ceases to govern action.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a secondary implication of graded competence and provides relevant contrary material, but does not defeat the capacity account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is clear and expressly qualified with probably and many, though action and decision categories are left partly unsettled.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly marks uncertainty and proposes the existence of such actions rather than claiming demonstrated prevalence.

charity.alternative: Microscopic differences may matter mainly when higher-level deliberation has already left multiple actions nearly equiprobable.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move must establish consequential sensitivity outside those knife-edge conditions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterpossibility is coherent, but its existence and frequency are asserted rather than derived from the preceding analysis.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move candidly offers a probable empirical claim but supplies no concrete evidence that tiny variations redirect non-balanced actions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the subsidiary luck bridge by extending microscopic contingency to consequential action.

representationalCharity.rationale: It states the knife-edge alternative accurately and directly identifies the empirical point on which it disagrees.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly rejects limiting bit flips to fifty-fifty decisions and suggests life-changing actions may hinge on tiny differences.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Libertarian free will maps onto neither determinism nor indeterminism, while graded lawful capacities constitute a compatibilist redefinition rather than the freedom denied by that dilemma.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris identifies the disagreement in first-person terms and contrasts his response with Dennett's account before introducing moral responsibility.

components.text: Whether compatibilist naturalization preserves free will or redefines it after conceding libertarian incoherence.
Whether responsibility-relevant freedom answers the incompatibilist dilemma rather than selecting a different phenomenon.
Whether graded lawful capacities exist and distinguish functioning agents.

response.rationale: The move concedes graded lawful capacities but directly argues that they are a redefinition because libertarian freedom maps onto neither causal option, contacting all three earlier conceptual components.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the conceptual preservation claim, the compatibility framing, and the reality of graded capacities.

precisionFindings.rationale: The deterministic dilemma, conceded capacity account, and alleged redefinition are clearly separated and consistently stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The incompatibility dilemma is asserted categorically but is supported as a conceptual exhaustive contrast rather than an empirical forecast.

charity.alternative: Compatibilism can openly revise an incoherent inherited concept while preserving its legitimate practical referent.
charity.decisiveQualification: The issue is whether the revision retains enough of the motivating phenomenon to count as preservation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument cleanly distinguishes the shared rejection of libertarianism from the disputed revisionary response without internal tension.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The deterministic-indeterministic dilemma and explicit concession provide strong support, though preservation criteria remain contested.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion-level claim that neither causal option supplies libertarian free will.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately concedes the compatibilist capacities and locates disagreement in the proper conceptual response to incoherence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that libertarian freedom maps onto neither determinism nor indeterminism and contrasts that view with graded compatibilist freedom.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Complete neurophysiological explanation would make ordinary wrongdoing exculpatory in the same relevant sense as behavior caused by a brain tumor because the decisive neural condition was not authored by the agent.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris introduces Charles Whitman, develops the neurological analogy, and explicitly generalizes it to ordinary neural causes before Dennett responds.

components.text: Whether responsibility remains justified when the decisive neural condition is fully explained and was not authored by the agent.
Whether ordinary competence supplies a principled distinction from neurologically caused impairment.

response.rationale: The move directly attacks responsibility preservation by generalizing the tumor-style exculpatory explanation to ordinary neurophysiology, while leaving practical capacity distinctions acknowledged but normatively insufficient.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive responsibility demand and supplies a clear leveling argument, though it does not fully answer competence-based distinctions.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is clearly conditional on complete neurophysiological understanding, making its otherwise universal scope explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The hypothetical premise is acknowledged, but the claim that explanation must exculpate ordinary agency like a tumor overstates the analogy.

charity.alternative: Tumors exculpate because they impair or bypass normal capacities, not merely because their causes can be explained.
charity.decisiveQualification: Universal exculpation requires showing that ordinary neural causation is relevantly equivalent to capacity-destroying pathology.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The causal leveling argument is intelligible, but it needs a major bridge showing why causal explanation erases capacity-based responsibility distinctions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The universal conclusion rests heavily on an analogy between ordinary synaptic causation and pathological impairment without comparative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central responsibility-gap bridge by separating causal production from genuine authorship.

representationalCharity.rationale: The brain-tumor analogy omits the strongest compatibilist distinction between normal functioning and capacity-undermining pathology.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly calls complete neurophysiology exculpatory, says it is brain tumors all the way down, and denies authorship of the decisive charge.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Differences in voluntary control and reasons-responsive capacity are real, but agents do not author the genes, environment, conversations, or prior brain states that determine those capacities and their responses.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris explicitly concedes differing capacities, then traces persuasion and character to prior causes and closes by preserving only pragmatic accountability.

components.text: Whether real differences in reasons-responsive capacity establish self-authorship despite their dependence on genes, environment, and prior brain states.
Whether responsibility-relevant capacities provide the authorship allegedly missing from causally produced responses.

response.rationale: The move explicitly concedes capacity differences and then attacks their authorship significance by tracing persuasion, character, and response to unchosen causal conditions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the strongest competence claim, grants its factual premise, and isolates the disputed inference to authorship.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between capacity, causal dependence, and pragmatic accountability is explicit and consistently maintained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The causal dependence claim is well framed, though saying a person does not pick any persuasive response compresses reflective feedback and attention.

charity.alternative: An agent can exercise authored control through capacities whose origins and implementation were not themselves chosen.
charity.decisiveQualification: The compatibilist must explain why unchosen capacity formation does not undermine the relevant form of authorship.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The concession-and-distinction structure is strong, with only a bounded gap from causal dependence to complete absence of authorship.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Genes, environment, conversations, and brain state provide specific causal categories, but the totalizing dependence claim is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central causal-nonauthorship bridge while engaging the opposing competence account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly grants the reality and practical importance of capacities while precisely disputing their self-authorship implications.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt traces persuasive reactions to genes, environmental influence, conversations, and the current brain state while denying that the reaction is picked.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Genuine control does not require control over every background condition; it consists in competently responding to given conditions and sustaining cultivated self-governance.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett introduces the control objection, develops the sailor and aircraft analogies, and extends the same principle through moral education and adult self-maintenance.

components.text: Whether genuine control requires control over the genes, environment, education, and background conditions producing one's capacities.
Whether dependence on uncontrolled microconditions defeats competent agent-level control.
Whether bounded control preserves a meaningful nonabsolute form of free agency.

response.rationale: The move directly rejects the demand for control of every condition and substitutes competent navigation and cultivated self-maintenance, while accepting degrees and diminished responsibility.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the causal-dependence objection and answers with a developed bounded-control criterion and impairment qualifications.

precisionFindings.rationale: Control is consistently defined as competent response rather than total causal command, with explicit allowances for incomplete responsibility.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move avoids absolute responsibility and expressly recognizes developmental failures and adults who are not fully responsible.

charity.alternative: The incompatibilist objection concerns authorship of the controller, not an impossible demand to control every external condition.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bounded control must explain how cultivated capacities qualify as authorship despite unchosen formation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogies consistently support a bounded conception of control, with one material bridge from effective navigation to moral authorship.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Sailing, aircraft, education, and adult maintenance give concrete support, though the analogy-to-responsibility warrant remains bounded.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central bounded-authorship bridge by explaining why control need not extend to all conditions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The answer is substantively fair but partly recasts the objection as total environmental control, leaving constitutive authorship underanswered.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span uses navigation and education examples, distinguishes control from control of all conditions, and explicitly allows diminished adult responsibility.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: A highly competent agent's rare failure may attract maximal blame while being least representative of that agent, exposing luck rather than stable competence as the explanation of the anomalous act.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris begins by conceding practical capacity distinctions, develops the Tiger Woods missed-putt case, and states the resulting paradox before yielding the floor.

components.text: Whether stable competence adequately explains and grounds blame for a rare anomalous failure by a highly capable agent.
Whether greater competence straightforwardly supports greater responsibility for an unrepresentative lapse.

response.rationale: The Tiger Woods analogy directly exposes a tension between competence, culpability, and representativeness, but it does not establish that moral lapses function exactly like missed putts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive implication of competence-based responsibility and develops a clear paradox, while leaving the moral analogy incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: The rare-lapse scenario and comparative claim are explicit, though culpability is used analogically rather than in its ordinary moral sense.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents luck as salient rather than conclusively proven, but the maximal-culpability formulation sharpens the analogy beyond its support.

charity.alternative: Competence grounds expectations while blame also depends on prior avoidability, reasons, stakes, and the kind of failure.
charity.decisiveQualification: A sports miss alone cannot establish how those additional moral variables operate.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The internal paradox is coherent, but the transfer from performance assessment to moral responsibility requires a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The vivid golf analogy supports the tension illustratively, but no representative moral case or alternative comparison is supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks competent-control sufficiency by testing how stable ability relates to anomalous failure.

representationalCharity.rationale: The analogy isolates a genuine tension but compresses the richer bases on which competence-sensitive moral blame may rest.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that the best golfer is most culpable for an easy miss even though the miss says least about his stable competence.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Relocating responsibility for an anomalous lapse to an earlier avoidable choice does not restore authorship, because closer examination makes each prior choice another causally produced, unauthored event.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris contrasts the first-person character of a lapse with Dennett's external account, then recursively applies the same causal objection to proposed prior explanations.

components.text: Whether relocating responsibility to an earlier avoidable choice resolves the authorship problem behind an anomalous lapse.
Whether a stable capacity history supplies authorship for each prior choice in the explanatory chain.

response.rationale: The move directly follows the proposed retreat to prior causes and argues that each earlier decision reintroduces the same unauthored-causation question.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the historical-control answer and states the regress consequence, although it does not refute bounded stopping criteria.

precisionFindings.rationale: The regress thesis is clear and stable, though it implicitly assumes the same ultimate-authorship standard at every prior stage.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The regress is forceful under ultimate authorship, but the move does not qualify its dependence on rejecting compatibilist historical control.

charity.alternative: Earlier choices can matter because they manifest settled capacities and create avoidable risks without requiring ultimate self-creation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must show why such bounded historical ownership is insufficient rather than merely nonultimate.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The regress follows coherently given the ultimate-authorship criterion, with one important unresolved dispute over that criterion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The anomalous-lapse discussion concretely motivates the regress, but no detailed prior-choice sequence tests rival stopping points.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It very directly supports the subsidiary luck-regress bridge by showing why prior choices may not restore authorship.

representationalCharity.rationale: It accurately addresses earlier-choice relocation but continues to apply the ultimate-authorship criterion without fully defending its necessity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls the lapse maximally adventitious and expressly says that going back to prior causes does not resolve the issue.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: People can author themselves within limits by working with unchosen materials and can accept moral responsibility even though luck contributes to their development and failures.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett immediately rejects absolute non-authorship, offers a bounded self-construction account, and carries the move into lookahead through his conclusion about unlucky conduct.

components.text: Whether any genuine self-authorship is possible without ultimate authorship of all starting materials and causal conditions.
Whether unchosen materials preclude a person from constructing and sustaining a moral self.
Whether acknowledged luck eliminates every meaningful degree of authorship.

response.rationale: The move directly rejects absolute nonauthorship by defining limited self-construction from found materials and openly conceding both limits and luck.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive regress premise and gives a qualified alternative conception, though its mechanism is only briefly developed.

precisionFindings.rationale: Bounded self-authorship is clearly stated, and both its limits and the role of luck are expressly acknowledged.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims only limited authorship and explicitly concedes found materials, luck, and practical constraints.

charity.alternative: The incompatibilist may accept self-modification while denying that it creates ultimate responsibility for the modifying dispositions.
charity.decisiveQualification: Bounded authorship answers only if ultimate responsibility is not required by the legitimate issue.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The found-materials model coherently avoids the false choice between total self-creation and no authorship, with a compressed sufficiency bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The do-it-yourself analogy and explicit concessions support bounded authorship, though sustained examples or rival comparison are absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central bounded-authorship bridge against the regress and constitutive-luck objections.

representationalCharity.rationale: The answer recognizes the force of luck and limitation, but it only briefly explains why bounded authorship is normatively sufficient.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says people author themselves using found objects, expressly limits do-it-yourself construction, and concedes substantial luck.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Responsibility need not be absolute because free will and legal accountability are pragmatic, consequentialist institutions calibrated to actual human capacities.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly accuses Harris of reverting to absolute responsibility and develops Dennett's consequentialist account of law and accountability.

components.text: Whether causal explanation defeats every justified form of responsibility or only absolute metaphysical desert.
Whether pragmatic accountability can remain justified without ultimate self-authorship.
Whether a consequentialist responsibility practice preserves the legitimate practical issue after libertarianism is rejected.

response.rationale: The move justifies replacing absolute responsibility with a consequentialist question about calibrated practices, preserving the legitimate concern with justified accountability while denying that ultimate desert is required.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the absolute-responsibility demand, explains the replacement standard, and states its institutional consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The rejection of absolute responsibility and adoption of consequentialist accountability are clearly separated and consistently qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move qualifies its consequentialism as more complex than deterrence and rehabilitation and avoids claiming absolute responsibility.

charity.alternative: The incompatibilist can support deterrence and rehabilitation while denying that these practices amount to genuine moral responsibility.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reframe must show that pragmatic accountability retains the legitimate content of responsibility rather than merely social control.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The consequentialist reframe is coherent and avoids dependence on absolute desert, with one bounded bridge about conceptual preservation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The institutional rationale is concrete but compressed, and detailed comparison with non-responsibility regulation remains incomplete.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central pragmatic-responsibility bridge through calibrated consequentialist accountability.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges the pragmatic concession but only partly answers the objection that the label responsibility changes normative content.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects absolute responsibility, calls free will pragmatic, and proposes a consequentialist rationale more complex than simple deterrence.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Even curable or causally diagnosed wrongdoing may warrant predictable penalties because deterrence, public confidence, and cooperative institutions depend on stable and enforceable rules.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker stresses recursive social effects, deterrence, respect for law, sports penalties, and the institutional importance of reliable sanctions.

components.text: Whether causal diagnosis or curability necessarily eliminates justified penalties and responsibility practices.
Whether predictable sanctions can be justified despite unchosen causal determinants of misconduct.

response.rationale: The move directly argues that causal explanation does not remove the institutional need for predictable rules and penalties, using deterrence, confidence, and cooperative practice as warrants.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the practical exculpation consequence strongly, though it answers institutional justification more fully than genuine authorship.

precisionFindings.rationale: The institutional claim is clear and bounded to predictable enforcement rather than unlimited punishment or absolute desert.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity claim is restricted to rule-governed cooperative practices, for which predictable enforcement is directly explained.

charity.alternative: An incompatibilist can endorse stable penalties instrumentally while denying that offenders deserve blame in an authorship-based sense.
charity.decisiveQualification: Institutional necessity alone does not establish ultimate desert or self-authorship.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from stable rules and penalties to viable cooperative institutions is explicit and internally consistent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Sports rules and predictable sanctions offer concrete support, though broader criminal-justice application needs further proportionality safeguards.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports pragmatic responsibility by explaining why reliable enforcement remains justified under causal explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not depend on ultimate desert and fairly concentrates on the practical responsibility conception it is defending.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses football rules and red-card penalties to explain why enjoyable cooperative practices require stable, enforceable sanctions.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Punishment and stable expectations can influence behavior, yet fuller causal understanding would reveal wrongdoing and reactions to it as unchosen brain states rather than genuine self-authorship.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker concedes deterrent utility before distinguishing the ethical and psychological issue, then develops Harris's predictive-neuroscience challenge to authorship.

components.text: Whether practical deterrence and stable enforcement establish genuine authorship or only useful behavioral regulation.
Whether consequentialist accountability preserves moral responsibility rather than merely justified social management.
Whether fuller causal understanding is compatible with the bounded authorship claimed by the agent-level account.

response.rationale: The move expressly concedes deterrence and practical governance, then distinguishes those functions from the ethical and psychological claim of authorship under fuller causal understanding.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the strongest institutional arguments, grants their practical conclusion, and precisely isolates the remaining authorship dispute.

precisionFindings.rationale: The concession to punishment's practical sense and the denial of authorship are clearly and consistently distinguished.

charity.alternative: Pragmatic responsibility may deliberately concern justified regulation and reliance rather than ultimate self-authorship.
charity.decisiveQualification: The disagreement then becomes whether those functions exhaust the legitimate content of moral responsibility.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Conscious authorship operates through temporally extended, high-level control and therefore does not require awareness or control of every neural microprocess implementing an action.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker rejects Harris's short-horizon prediction case and uses Mozart, tennis, and jazz examples characteristic of Dennett's macro-control account.

components.text: Whether unconscious neural implementation and possible prior prediction eliminate conscious authorship at the temporally extended agent level.
Whether lack of microlevel control defeats high-level ownership of an action-producing process.
Whether organized, temporally extended control can constitute authorship despite causal dependence.

response.rationale: The move directly rejects microprocess awareness as the standard for ownership and supplies Mozart, tennis, and improvisation examples of extended high-level control.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the nonauthorship inference and provides a developed alternative level of explanation rather than merely asserting compatibility.

precisionFindings.rationale: Microlevel and temporally extended macrolevel control are consistently distinguished, with ownership claimed only to a degree.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move explicitly says agents control processes to some degree and avoids claiming awareness or command of every neural event.

charity.alternative: Prediction before conscious awareness may suggest consciousness reports a decision rather than authors the process producing it.
charity.decisiveQualification: Prediction does not defeat authorship if the predicted process belongs to the agent's extended control system.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The levels-of-control distinction is explicit, consistent, and resolves the immediate inference from unconscious implementation to nonauthorship.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Mozart, tennis, and improvisation provide specific convergent examples, with only a bounded gap in generalizing to all responsible action.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central bounded-authorship bridge through a temporally extended account of agent-level control.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move addresses the strongest prediction-based interpretation and states the relevant agent-level qualification directly.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt attributes compositions to Mozart because they arose in his controlled processes and contrasts microlevel control with temporally macro control.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: An agent could have done otherwise by possessing competence across a real range of actions, without requiring an atom-for-atom replay of the identical physical universe.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly demurs from Harris's conclusion and articulates Dennett's capacity-based interpretation of alternative possibilities and causation.

components.text: Whether doing otherwise must mean divergence in an atom-for-atom identical replay or competence across a real action range.
Whether a capacity-based alternative preserves the legitimate action-guiding content after libertarian replay freedom is rejected.
Whether a bit-level difference is compatible with possessing a broader competence to act otherwise.

response.rationale: The move justifies replacing exact physical replay with a competence-across-circumstances criterion, preserving the legitimate issue of what actions the agent can reliably perform.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the replay demand, supplies the replacement criterion, and explains why exact replication is irrelevant to practical ability.

precisionFindings.rationale: The competence sense of could have done otherwise is explicit and sharply contrasted with atom-for-atom replication.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conceptual claim is categorical but supported by the explicit distinction between ability and exact historical replay.

charity.alternative: The incompatibilist seeks actual divergence under exactly the same total conditions, not merely a stable general competence.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply must explain why that stronger demand lacks relevance to the legitimate control question.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The reframe cleanly separates token outcome from general ability and states why exact replay is not required by the latter.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The action-range distinction strongly supports the conceptual conclusion, though no difficult impairment case tests its boundaries.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly supplies the subsidiary alternatives bridge through a competence-based interpretation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move states the exact-replay alternative accurately and directly argues that it is irrelevant to real-world competence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says an agent has a real range of abilities and rejects atom-for-atom replication as irrelevant to that sense of otherwise.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Neither deterministic chaos nor practical randomization supplies upstream ownership, and sufficiently early neural prediction would expose conscious action as the result rather than the author of its causal process.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker distinguishes coin flipping from true freedom and returns to Harris's recurring claims about upstream causes, conscious awareness, and predictive neuroscience.

components.text: Whether a range of competencies or practical randomness supplies upstream ownership of the action-producing process.
Whether sufficiently early prediction would undermine rather than merely reveal temporally extended agent-level authorship.
Whether bounded control answers the felt demand for upstream ownership.

response.rationale: The move contacts the competence and macro-authorship answers by separating randomization from ownership and arguing that prior neural prediction would challenge conscious authorship.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts two decisive replies, but the prediction premise is hypothetical and does not fully answer system-level ownership.

precisionFindings.rationale: Randomness, upstream ownership, conscious awareness, and hypothetical prediction are distinctly stated with an explicit conditional.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The experimental scenario is expressly hypothetical, but the predicted public and philosophical impact is asserted more broadly than supported.

charity.alternative: Early prediction can track the agent's own extended process without showing that consciousness is a separate nonauthoring spectator.
charity.decisiveQualification: The timing evidence must distinguish prediction of authorship from prediction by observing the authoring system.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Randomness not implying ownership is strong, but prediction before awareness does not by itself entail absence of system-level authorship.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The randomness point is conceptually supported, while the decisive neuroimaging scenario remains hypothetical and underverified.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary randomness-prediction bridge by denying that chance or prediction creates ownership.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move raises the right ownership challenge but does not fully engage the strongest temporally extended system interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt denies upstream ownership from practical randomness and says advance neuroimaging prediction would challenge felt authorship of creative and volitional action.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: The difference between deterministic chaos and quantum indeterminacy makes no moral difference, so indeterminacy supplies no freedom unavailable from deterministic processes.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn begins with an explicit statement of disagreement and continues uninterrupted until Harris answers the moral-difference claim.

components.text: Whether quantum indeterminacy provides morally relevant freedom that deterministic chaos merely imitates.
Whether indeterminism supplies any freedom unavailable under deterministic processes.

response.rationale: The move identifies the alleged real-randomness distinction and defeats its relevance by stating that deterministic chaos and quantum indeterminacy make no moral difference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly names the premise, denies its moral relevance, and states the defeating consequence for freedom.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison between deterministic chaos and quantum indeterminacy is explicit and limited to moral significance.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical moral-equivalence claim is clear but supported only briefly rather than through a developed comparison of consequences.

charity.alternative: Real indeterminacy differs metaphysically from deterministic unpredictability even if neither grants ownership.
charity.decisiveQualification: A metaphysical difference matters here only if it changes control, authorship, or moral responsibility.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The diagnostic inference is clean: a physical distinction that changes no morally relevant control cannot supply additional moral freedom.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The moral-irrelevance rationale is plausible and precise, though the excerpt does not extensively compare possible rival implications.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly completes the subsidiary indeterminacy bridge by denying any morally relevant gain from quantum randomness.
